title: New York Times Investigation Says Jensen Huang Used Humiliation as a Management Tool
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Jensen Huang repeatedly berated Nvidia employees in front of colleagues, using insults and personal attacks that he portrayed as motivation, according to a November 20 investigation by The New York Times. The report said Nvidia’s co-founder “used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers.” It drew on interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, as well as court records and other documents spanning more than two decades.

That humiliation allegedly took many forms. One employee reported that Huang "said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and 'pee on your brain'."

Some employees told the Times that Nvidia’s human resources department failed to take workplace complaints seriously. The investigation also reported that Nvidia paid more than $1 million in a confidential settlement with former executive Michael Winston, who alleged that the company fired him for objecting to Huang’s treatment of employees. Neither side admitted liability or wrongdoing in the settlement. Nvidia declined to comment on the Times investigation.

The accounts illustrate how differently employees experienced Huang’s leadership. Some described a boss who dressed people down in meetings and made criticism personal. Others recalled a leader who noticed individual contributions and offered support during difficult times. After Huang resigned, senior Nvidia employee Nader Khalil urged the board to bring him back, warning that some employees were considering leaving, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation on November 12 and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO while it searches for a permanent successor. Board chair Harvey C. Jones has said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. The leadership transition puts a question about Nvidia’s day-to-day culture in front of Kress and the board. Huang favored a flat structure and defended group meetings as a way to increase transparency. The employee accounts describe how those same meetings could expose staff to ridicule in front of the colleagues they worked with every day.
